lines.en: What we call 'normal' is usually nothing more than the habits of the people we grew up around.
It is possible to leave your country without ever leaving your culture, and to lose your culture without ever leaving home.
Were every culture to see itself through a stranger's eyes, the world would quarrel far less.
However global the world becomes, people still dream in the language of their childhood.
Not until you live abroad do you discover which parts of you are you, and which are your country.
It is often the smallest customs - a greeting, a meal, a song - that carry the deepest sense of belonging.
What the immigrant packs last and never unpacks is a way of being polite.
The proverb is said to be the shortest road to a culture's heart.
Little by little, the children of immigrants build a self that belongs fully to neither world and wholly to both.
Rarely does anyone choose their culture, yet everyone is judged by it.
What the third-generation child inherits is not the language of the grandparents but its echo.
It is at weddings and funerals, not in museums, that a culture shows what it truly is.
Were accents to disappear, every language would lose the map of its own history.
Not until we taste another culture's celebrations do we realize that our own are also strange and wonderful.
However modern a society becomes, its oldest stories keep whispering in its newest songs.
